claim: The ISS is designed and operated to approximate an Earth-equivalent cabin atmosphere of 14.7 psia with 21% oxygen.
quote: The ISS was designed and is operated to approximate an Earth-equivalent atmosphere of 14.7 psia with 21% O2.
source_title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures (NASA/TM-20260003925, NESC-RP-20-01610)
source_authors: Morgan B. Abney; Robert M. Bagdigian; Chase Hopkins; Ariel V. Macatangay; Holly A. Cagle; Michael D. Pedley; James Knox
source_org: NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC), Langley Research Center
limits: Nominal design point only; the same paragraph gives a control band and a maximum allowable O2 (separate claim). Says nothing about the ISS airlock, which is run at lower pressure before spacewalks.
usefulness: (a) Origin atmosphere of the demo item: what ISS-certified equipment was designed and certified for (1.00 atm, 21% O2).
verifier_note: Quote exact on PDF p. 18 (report p. 14, footer 'Page #: 14 of 15'). Context supports the claim as worded; NTRS record (NASA/TM-20260003925, NESC-RP-20-01610, May 2026, 7 authors) matches title/authors/year. Landing and PDF URLs open.

claim: The ISS environmental control system is designed to hold the cabin within 13.9-15.2 psia and an O2 partial pressure of 2.83-3.35 psia, with a maximum allowable oxygen of 24.1 vol%.
quote: The ISS environmental control system is designed to control the cabin atmosphere within the bands of 13.9-15.2 psia and O2 partial pressure of 2.83-3.35 psia with a maximum allowable of 24.1 vol% O2
source_title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures (NASA/TM-20260003925, NESC-RP-20-01610)
source_authors: Morgan B. Abney; Robert M. Bagdigian; Chase Hopkins; Ariel V. Macatangay; Holly A. Cagle; Michael D. Pedley; James Knox
source_org: NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC), Langley Research Center
limits: Design control band as cited by the report from its reference 5; it is an equipment-control limit, not an ignition threshold of any material. Does not describe the airlock during prebreathe.
usefulness: (a)(c) The oxygen ceiling that ISS-certified cargo can assume in the cabin (24.1%); an operational max-O2 limit. Anything flown to a 26-37% O2 destination leaves this envelope.
verifier_note: Quote exact, same paragraph as the nominal claim. The report attributes the band to its ref. 5 (NASA/TP-2010-216134), so it is a cited design band, not a new measurement. The next sentence says all other on-board equipment is designed and certified within these ranges, which is the basis of the passport logic.

claim: The STS-133 press kit (February 2011) describes the ISS campout prebreathe plan as: the two spacewalkers isolate themselves inside the airlock while its air pressure is lowered to 10.2 psi, and the station is kept at 14.7 psi.
quote: isolate themselves inside the airlock while the air pressure is lowered to 10.2 pounds per square inch (psi). The station is kept at the near-sea-level pressure of 14.7 psi.
source_title: Space Shuttle Mission STS-133 Press Kit (The Final Flight of Discovery)
source_authors: NASA
source_org: NASA
limits: Press-kit description of the planned campout for one mission's spacewalkers (STS-133, February 2011). Gives pressure only, not the oxygen percentage in the airlock. kPa is our conversion.
usefulness: (a)(b) Shows the ISS airlock is run at a different pressure than the cabin before spacewalks; pair with the ECLSS TM claim that the airlock during EVA prebreathe is the worst-case flammability condition (30% O2 at 10.2 psia, = 0.69 atm).
verifier_note: Quote exact (press-kit p. 40, PDF p. 44). Narrowed: the sentence is a plan for the STS-133 spacewalkers (Bowen and Drew, Feb 2011), not a general statement about every campout; claim now says so. No oxygen percentage is given anywhere in the passage.

claim: In the Space Shuttle staged-decompression protocol, the cabin was lowered to 10.2 psia (70.2 kPa) with 26.5% oxygen after one hour of oxygen prebreathe.
quote: In the staged decompression protocol, the crewmembers perform 1 hour of oxygen prebreathe before depressing the cabin to 10.2 psia (70.2 kPa) with 26.5% oxygen.
source_title: Biomedical Support of U.S. Extravehicular Activity
source_authors: M. L. Gernhardt; J. P. Dervay; D. Gillis; H. J. McMann; K. S. Thomas
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center (preprint)
locator: PDF p. 2 (discussion of Shuttle EVA decompression protocols)
limits: Physiology/EVA-operations description from a 2007 preprint; not a flammability result. The same paper describes an ISS airlock 'campout' at 10.2 psia (p. 3) but states the 26.5% O2 only for the Shuttle case.
usefulness: (a)(c) Gives the nominal O2 that goes with 10.2 psia (0.69 atm): 26.5%, not 30%. 30% is the materials-certification ceiling for this atmosphere (see other claims).
verifier_note: Quote exact on PDF p. 2. NTRS 20080000344 is a 2007 preprint (Gernhardt, Dervay, Gillis, McMann, Thomas) and the title/authors match. The passage is about the Shuttle cabin; 26.5% is stated for the Shuttle case only.

claim: NASA has extensive 1-g flammability data on polymeric materials at 24.1% O2 and 14.7 psia (the ISS maximum except in the airlock during EVA prebreathe) and at 30% O2 and 10.2 psia (the worst case for the Shuttle orbiter, the ISS airlock during EVA prebreathe, Orion's crew module and Commercial Crew vehicles).
quote: NASA has extensive 1-g data on polymeric materials flammability in 24.1% O2 at 14.7 psia (e.g., ISS maximum O2 concentration other than in the airlock during EVA prebreathe) and 30% O2 at 10.2 psia (the worst-case conditions for materials flammability in the SSP orbiter, the ISS Airlock during EVA prebreathe, MPCV CM, and CCP vehicles).
source_title: Impacts of Reduced Pressure Atmospheres on Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) Architectures (NASA/TM-20260003925, NESC-RP-20-01610)
source_authors: Morgan B. Abney; Robert M. Bagdigian; Chase Hopkins; Ariel V. Macatangay; Holly A. Cagle; Michael D. Pedley; James Knox
source_org: NASA Engineering and Safety Center (NESC), Langley Research Center

conditions.pressure_text: 10.2 psia (worst case); 24.1% O2 at 14.7 psia is the ISS cabin maximum

limits: These are test and certification envelope conditions, not the nominal cabin atmosphere (nominal at 10.2 psia is 26.5% O2). All the data are 1-g; sample thickness and form are not given in this sentence. MPCV CM = Orion crew module; CCP = Commercial Crew Program.
usefulness: (a)(b)(c) States exactly where '30% O2 at 10.2 psia (0.694 atm, our conversion)' comes from and names the ISS airlock during EVA prebreathe as the highest-O2 zone of the ISS.
verifier_note: Quote exact (report p. 29, PDF p. 33). Claim did not say the data are for polymeric materials and read as if all flammability data sit at these two points; narrowed to 'extensive 1-g data on polymeric materials' as in the source. Acronyms SSP, MPCV CM and CCP are expanded in the report's own Table 1 (Sec. 6.1).

claim: NASA's Orion crew module was being designed for an atmosphere of up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia for lunar missions.
quote: The Orion Crew Exploration Vehicle Module (CM) is being designed to operate in an atmosphere of up to 30% oxygen at a pressure of 10.2 psia for lunar missions.
source_title: Pressure Effects on the Self-Extinguishment Limits of Aerospace Materials (SAE 09ICES-0267, JSC-17943)
source_authors: David B. Hirsch; James H. Williams; Jon P. Haas; Harold D. Beeson; Gary A. Ruff; Michael D. Pedley
source_org: NASA White Sands Test Facility / Johnson Space Center
limits: Abstract-only source (no full text on NTRS). A 2009 Constellation-era design statement for Orion's crew module, not a current Artemis requirement and not a lunar base or lander atmosphere. The abstract says materials are certified at 30% O2 and 10.2 psia because oxygen concentration is the primary driver.
usefulness: (a) Closest direct NASA statement of a '30% O2, 10.2 psia (0.69 atm)' pair for a lunar-mission vehicle. Answers the team's open question: the pair exists, but as an Orion design/certification point.
verifier_note: Quote exact in the NTRS 20090012334 abstract (read from the NTRS JSON record, full text not hosted). Title, six authors (Hirsch, Williams, Haas, Beeson, Ruff, Pedley), SAE 09ICES-0267 / JSC-17943 and the July 2009 ICES conference all match. Past-tense wording in the claim ('was being designed') is correct for a Constellation-era statement.

claim: The Exploration Atmospheres Working Group recommended that, for lunar sortie missions, the docked crew vehicle and lander operate at a nominal 10.2 psia and 26.5% oxygen.
quote: For lunar sortie missions, the docked CEV and lander (also known as lunar surface access module [LSAM)], should operate at a nominal 10.2 psia total pressure, 26.5% oxygen concentration.
source_title: Recommendations for Exploration Spacecraft Internal Atmospheres: The Final Report of the NASA Exploration Atmospheres Working Group (NASA/TP-2010-216134)
source_authors: NASA Exploration Atmospheres Working Group
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center
limits: 2010 Constellation-era recommendation; the report states 'The recommendations provided herein are not requirements and reflect technical considerations only.' The lander is called LSAM here; Altair is not named in this sentence. The same report recommends 8.0 psia/32% O2 for lander surface operations.
usefulness: (a)(b) Sourced atmosphere for a lunar lander while docked: 0.69 atm and 26.5% O2. Explains the 10.2 psia half of the video's pair.
verifier_note: Quote exact on PDF p. 11 (printed p. 1, Executive Summary). The report is NASA/TP-2010-216134, October 2010; the same paragraph states the recommendations 'are not requirements', already in limits. The same section recommends 8.0 psia / 32% O2 for surface landers, which is not part of this claim.

claim: NASA Artemis requirements for sustained missions target an average pressure of 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) and 34% oxygen.
quote: NASA Artemis requirements for sustained missions are targeting an average pressure of 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) and a 34% oxygen concentration as one solution to those trade-offs.
source_title: Surface Vehicle Atmospheric Considerations for Moon to Mars Exploration (ICES-2026-324)
source_authors: Brian K. Alpert; Logan Kennedy; L. Daren Welsh; Adam Young; Gregory L. Mercer; Daniel S. Baird
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center / Marshall Space Flight Center (55th International Conference on Environmental Systems)
limits: Described in the paper as 'one solution to those trade-offs'; the paper adds that less is known above 30% O2 and that NASA teams also test a vehicle atmosphere below 30%. Sustained missions only, not the first landings.
usefulness: (a)(c) Current NASA target for a lunar habitat/lander: 0.56 atm and 34% O2 (13 points more oxygen than the ISS cabin).
verifier_note: Quote exact on PDF p. 3. NTRS 20260002050 = ICES-2026-324 (55th ICES, July 2026; six authors match). The same paragraph adds that NASA teams also tested a vehicle atmosphere below 30% (9.6 psi, 28.5% O2), already noted in limits.

Claim reworded from 'options' to the paper's 'architectures'. MOC is a testing ceiling, not nominal cabin O2 (paper: 34% atmosphere tested up to 37%).

claim: NASA's exploration EVA concept of operations says the pressurized rover will be capable of operating at nominal cabin set points of 14.7 psia/21% O2, 10.2 psia/27% O2 and 8.2 psia/34% O2.
quote: The rover will be capable of operating at the following nominal cabin atmosphere saturation set points: • 14.7 psia with 21% O2 • 10.2 psia with 27% O2 • 8.2 psia and 34% O2
source_title: Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations (EVA-EXP-0042, Revision B)
source_authors: David Coan (prepared by); NASA EVA Office
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center, EVA Office

Replaced by the layout-faithful wording with one bullet per item; evtool finds it in the layout text of PDF p. 65 and the PDF page shows a three-item bullet list under that sentence. Values (21%, 27%, 34%) are exactly as the source states them.

claim: Lower vehicle pressure can shorten spacewalk prebreathe because less nitrogen is dissolved in the body, but it usually needs a higher oxygen concentration to prevent hypoxia, which carries higher flammability risk.
quote: Lower vehicle pressures can reduce prebreathe time by reducing the initial amount of dissolved nitrogen in the body but they usually require higher oxygen concentrations (higher flammability risk) to prevent hypoxia.
source_title: Surface Vehicle Atmospheric Considerations for Moon to Mars Exploration (ICES-2026-324)
source_authors: Brian K. Alpert; Logan Kennedy; L. Daren Welsh; Adam Young; Gregory L. Mercer; Daniel S. Baird
source_org: NASA Johnson Space Center / Marshall Space Flight Center (55th International Conference on Environmental Systems)

limits: Qualitative statement; the paper gives no flammability threshold here. 'Higher flammability risk' is not quantified in this sentence.
usefulness: (c) The causal chain for the demo: low pressure -> prebreathe shorter -> O2 % must rise -> materials burn more readily (decompression sickness vs hypoxia vs fire trade).
verifier_note: Quote exact (PDF p. 5). Source says lower pressures 'can reduce' prebreathe time and 'usually require' higher O2; the claim said 'shortens'. Softened to 'can shorten' to match the modality of the source.

claim: The NESC assessment found that materials had to change in 21% of the assessed ISS-heritage subsystems for 10.2 psia/26.5% O2 and in 70% of them for 8.2 psia/34% O2.

usefulness: (a) Quantifies how much ISS-certified hardware stops being acceptable as O2 rises: about 1 in 5 at 26.5%, about 7 in 10 at 34%.

The same section confirms the scope: 33 subsystems/components of ISS ECLS hardware, assessed from design data and historical literature, 10.2 psia/26.5% O2 and 8.2 psia/34% O2 (up to 40% O2 for flammability). claim: NASA has flammability data for many materials at 30% O2 but limited data above it, and many commonly used ISS materials are flammable above 30% O2.
quote: NASA has data for many materials in a 30% O2 environment, but limited material flammability data above this O2 limit. Further, many commonly used ISS materials are flammable above 30% O2.

limits: Qualitative statement; no per-material thresholds in this sentence. Says nothing about partial gravity.

claim: ISS materials shown to meet flammability requirements at 10.2 psia and 30% O2 but unlikely to meet them at higher O2 include polymeric materials, foam insulations (Armaflex, Solimide AC-550), Bisco HT-200 silicone and Soundcoat HT polyimide foam.
quote: Many ISS materials have been shown to meet flammability requirements at 10.2 psia and 30% O2, but are unlikely to meet the requirements at higher O2 concentrations. Materials in this category include polymeric materials, foam thermal insulations (e.g., Armaflex and Solimide AC-550 polyimide), Bisco HT-200 sound block silicone, Soundcoat HT polyimide foam

claim: NASA states that a flame can be extinguished when cabin airflow is high enough, that this happens more readily on Earth because higher gravity causes higher flow velocities, and that a material that self-extinguishes in Earth gravity may continue to burn in lunar gravity.
quote: A flame can extinguish if the cabin airflow is high enough that the reactants don't have time to react while the mixture is hot enough. This effect occurs more readily on Earth because the higher gravity causes higher flow velocities. Thus, a material that self-extinguishes in Earth gravity may continue to burn in lunar gravity.

limits: Qualitative reasoning, no thresholds, and the paper cites a NASA podcast interview for the point (its reference 5). The ECLSS TM (report p. 29) likewise says 'limited data' suggest more flammability in partial gravity and that essentially all flammability test data are 1-g.
usefulness: (c) Links gravity level and airflow speed to flammability; the reason a ground (1 g) pass does not carry over to the Moon.
verifier_note: Quote exact (PDF p. 4; three consecutive sentences). Reference [5] in the paper is a NASA 'Houston We Have a Podcast' episode (23 May 2025), so the statement is reasoning reported by NASA authors, not a test result; limits already say so.
